prompt: Surface energy γ exists because:
options: Atoms move faster at the surface than in bulk
Surface atoms have unsatisfied bonds
Light reflects off surfaces, transferring energy
Pressure varies with height above the surface
explanation: Creating new surface costs the energy of unsatisfied bonds. Liquids minimize area to minimize energy — that's why drops are spheres.

prompt: A contact angle of θ = 5° (water on glass) indicates:
options: Strongly hydrophobic surface that repels water
Strongly hydrophilic surface; water wets readily
Vacuum boundary with no liquid present
An ordinary clean uncoated solid surface
correctAnswer: Strongly hydrophilic surface; water wets readily
explanation: Small θ → water spreads. Large θ (>150°) → superhydrophobic, water beads off. Contact angle is set by the balance of solid-liquid, solid-vapor, and liquid-vapor interfacial tensions.

prompt: Why is gold catalytic only when in nanoparticle form?
options: Bulk gold is too dense and heavy for catalysis
Nanoparticles are mostly surface, not bulk
The colour of nano-gold differs from bulk gold
Magnetic effects appear only at the nanoscale
correctAnswer: Nanoparticles are mostly surface, not bulk
explanation: Bulk gold is famously inert. 5-nm Au nanoparticles catalyze CO oxidation at room temperature. The size dependence is striking — surface fraction and quantum effects both matter.

prompt: The lotus effect creates self-cleaning surfaces by combining superhydrophobicity with microscale roughness.
explanation: Water beads roll off; the surface texture means droplets touch only the tops of the bumps, picking up dirt particles as they roll. Inspired self-cleaning paints, fabrics, and glass.

prompt: Match the surface property to its everyday consequence:

pairs.right: Water rolls off into beads — lotus leaf
Drops form spheres to minimize area

explanation: Surface chemistry shows up everywhere — kitchens, clothes, technology, biology. Tuning contact angles is one of materials science's classic levers.

prompt: The key difference between physisorption and chemisorption is:
options: The colour visible under standard lighting
Bond strength: van der Waals vs chemical bond
Whether it occurs in vacuum environments
Whether the underlying surface is a metal
correctAnswer: Bond strength: van der Waals vs chemical bond
explanation: Physisorption: 5–50 kJ/mol, reversible, no structural changes. Chemisorption: 100–500 kJ/mol, often dissociative (H₂ → 2H), step before catalytic reaction.

prompt: BET analysis of N₂ adsorption is used to measure:
options: The colour of finely divided solids in air
Porous-material surface area, accurately
Heat capacity of the porous solid sample
Magnetic susceptibility of the bulk material
explanation: Brunauer-Emmett-Teller theory extends Langmuir to multilayer adsorption. Activated carbons, zeolites, and MOFs commonly have BET surface areas of 1000–7000 m²/g — measured precisely by N₂ at 77 K.

prompt: When H₂ chemisorbs on a platinum surface, the molecule typically:
options: Stays intact, weakly bound to a single site
Dissociates into two H atoms each surface-bound
Becomes ionised into H⁺ and an electron pair
Reflects off the surface without binding at all
correctAnswer: Dissociates into two H atoms each surface-bound
explanation: Dissociative chemisorption is common on metals. The surface lowers the H-H bond's effective energy by binding the products. This is the first step in many hydrogenation reactions.

prompt: Surface diffusion of adsorbed atoms can be observed in real time with scanning tunneling microscopy.
explanation: STM movies of metal adatoms diffusing on metal surfaces are now routine. The hopping rate gives diffusion barriers, and reactions between adatoms can be watched directly.

prompt: Match each adsorption mode/measurement to its description:

pairs.right: Multilayer adsorption — used to measure surface area

explanation: Adsorption theory provides the foundation for all surface chemistry. Quantitative isotherms turn surface science into a measurable, predictive discipline.

prompt: The Haber-Bosch process produces:
options: Concentrated sulfuric acid for industry
Ammonia (NH₃), used as a nitrogen fertilizer
Hydrogen gas for industrial chemistry
Methanol from carbon monoxide and hydrogen
correctAnswer: Ammonia (NH₃), used as a nitrogen fertilizer
explanation: N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃ on Fe at ~400 °C and 200 atm. ~150 million tonnes/year. Roughly half the nitrogen in the bodies of all 8 billion people came through Haber-Bosch.

prompt: Catalytic converters use which precious metals?
options: Gold and silver, plated onto a steel mesh
Platinum, palladium, rhodium on porous ceramic
Lead and tin alloyed onto cordierite supports
Aluminium and iron oxides as solid pellets
correctAnswer: Platinum, palladium, rhodium on porous ceramic
explanation: These three are the workhorses. Platinum and palladium oxidize CO and hydrocarbons; rhodium reduces NOx. Demand from automobiles drives most platinum-group metal mining.

prompt: Sabatier's principle says the best catalyst:
options: Binds reaction intermediates as strongly as possible
Binds intermediates with intermediate strength
Binds nothing and merely concentrates the reagents
Has the largest possible accessible surface area
explanation: Too weak: no activation. Too strong: poisoning, slow desorption. The optimum is at the volcano-plot peak. Modern computational catalysis maps these volcanoes to discover new catalysts.

prompt: Haber-Bosch consumes 1-2% of total global energy.
explanation: Mostly from the natural-gas-fed steam reforming that supplies hydrogen. Renewable-electricity-driven nitrogen reduction is a major research goal — a green Haber-Bosch would cut a substantial slice of global emissions.

prompt: Match the catalytic process to its application:

pairs.right: Refining crude oil into gasoline and chemicals

explanation: Heterogeneous catalysis quietly underpins much of modern industry. Each of these examples is a multi-billion-dollar process built around surface chemistry.

prompt: A self-assembled monolayer (SAM) of thiols on gold forms because:
options: Sulfur atoms melt the gold surface locally
Au-S bonds anchor the molecules; chains pack via vdW
Strong magnetic forces order the molecules
Gravity orients the chains away from the surface
correctAnswer: Au-S bonds anchor the molecules; chains pack via vdW
explanation: The thiol head sticks via S-Au; alkyl tails align by minimizing chain-chain energy. Surface properties are then dictated by whatever group terminates the chain (CH₃, OH, COOH, etc.).

prompt: Lipid nanoparticles delivered the mRNA in COVID vaccines because:
options: The lipids are radioactively tagged for tracking
They self-assemble into mRNA-protecting vesicles
They glow under standard tissue imaging conditions
Their high mass enables passive cellular delivery
explanation: Cationic lipids package negatively-charged mRNA. The vesicles fuse with cells, releasing mRNA inside. Self-assembled lipid biophysics scaled to billions of doses in months.

prompt: Block copolymers self-assemble into:
options: Random tangles with no long-range order
Ordered nanostructures (lamellae, gyroids)
Single perfect crystals at all chain lengths
Gas-phase mixtures of monomers and polymers
explanation: Microphase separation of immiscible blocks gives periodic patterns at 10–100 nm. Used as templates for nanolithography below the optical diffraction limit. Composition and chain length set morphology.

prompt: Self-assembly relies entirely on covalent bonds.
explanation: Self-assembly typically uses non-covalent forces: hydrogen bonds, van der Waals, hydrophobic effects, electrostatics. That's what allows reversibility, self-correction, and equilibration toward an ordered structure.

prompt: Match the self-assembled structure to its example:
explanation: Three classes of self-assembly span chemistry, biology, and materials science. They share thermodynamic principles — and underpin technologies from biosensors to vaccines.

prompt: MOFs (metal-organic frameworks) achieve enormous surface area because they are:
options: Solid blocks of metal alloy with no porosity
Crystalline metal-linker frameworks with pores
Liquid solutions of metal-organic complexes
Gases of metal atoms paired with organic ligands
explanation: MOFs literally are scaffolds with pores by design. Some have BET areas exceeding 7000 m²/g — a single gram with more surface than a tennis court. Used for gas storage, separations, catalysis.

prompt: Single-atom catalysts:
options: Use only one atom of metal in the entire reactor
Disperse metal atoms one-at-a-time on a support
Are made from a single element with no support
Are illegal under modern catalysis regulations
correctAnswer: Disperse metal atoms one-at-a-time on a support
explanation: Maximum atom utilization. Pt single atoms on N-doped carbon, Cu single atoms on ceria — these can match or exceed nanoparticle activity at far lower metal loading. Stability is the engineering challenge.

prompt: Why is electrocatalysis a green-chemistry priority?
options: It uses no chemicals during normal operation
It can replace stoichiometric reagents with electrons
It runs faster than conventional chemical processes
It is significantly cheaper than thermal catalysis
correctAnswer: It can replace stoichiometric reagents with electrons
explanation: Hydrogen evolution, CO₂ reduction, ammonia synthesis, water oxidation — all can in principle run on solar or wind electricity, replacing fossil-fueled or stoichiometric chemistry.

prompt: Photocatalysis uses sunlight directly to drive surface reactions.
explanation: Semiconductors (TiO₂ classically, plus newer materials) absorb photons and create electron-hole pairs that drive surface redox chemistry. Practical solar fuels — water splitting and CO₂ reduction — remain hard but progressing.

prompt: Match each frontier surface-chemistry concept to its key feature:

pairs.right: Maximum atom utilization, often unique selectivity

explanation: Modern surface chemistry is a meeting point for materials science, catalysis, and renewable energy. Each concept here is reshaping how chemistry meets sustainability.
